title: Iran and Israel Say They Have Stopped Shooting. India Says It Is Watching.
excerpt: New Delhi expressed utmost concern as missiles flew. The Strait of Hormuz is still closed. Oil is still near $97.
body:
India's foreign ministry expressed "utmost concern" on Monday as Iran and Israel traded missiles, drones, and airstrikes over a 36-hour period — the most direct military exchange between the two countries since a fragile U.S.-brokered ceasefire took hold in April. Hours later, both sides said they had halted operations.

For New Delhi, the timing is brutal. Brent crude surged past $97 a barrel before settling near $94, oil imports through the Strait of Hormuz remain effectively frozen, and Indian equity markets slid to two-month lows on the back of the fresh hostilities.

## What Happened

Iran fired multiple barrages of missiles at Israeli territory late Sunday, calling them retaliation for Israeli strikes on Hezbollah positions near Beirut. Israel responded by hitting Iranian air defence systems and a petrochemical facility it said was used for ballistic missile production. The IRGC then struck what it described as a similar Israeli facility in Haifa.

No casualties were reported on either side.

U.S. President Donald Trump intervened directly, telling Fox News: "You've shot your missiles, that's enough. Get back to the table and make a deal." On Truth Social, he wrote that both sides were "looking to do an immediate CEASEFIRE." In an Axios interview, Trump revealed he had warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu: "Bibi, you better be careful, or you will be on your own very soon."

By Monday afternoon, Iran's military command said its operations had concluded. A source briefed on the matter confirmed Israel had also decided to halt strikes. But Iran warned it would resume hostilities if Israel continued targeting Hezbollah in Lebanon.

## India's Balancing Act

The Ministry of External Affairs issued a pointed statement calling on "all parties to immediately de-escalate tensions and conclude ongoing negotiations for a diplomatic solution." It stopped short of naming either side — consistent with India's carefully calibrated posture throughout the conflict.

India's stakes are enormous. Before the war, more than 40% of India's crude imports and roughly 90% of its LPG supplies transited the Strait of Hormuz. That route has been effectively shut since fighting erupted in February, forcing India to scramble for Western Hemisphere alternatives at a steep premium.

Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri told CNN-News18 on Monday that India has reserves for 76 to 80 days and expects prices to fall in the months ahead. But he acknowledged the situation could become "worrying" if the Gulf crisis expands further.

## The Economic Fallout

Indian state fuel retailers have raised prices four times since mid-May. Petrol is up 7.8%, diesel 8.6%. The RBI held rates last week but launched a $50 billion defence package — including concessional swaps on NRI deposits — to shore up the rupee, which has been battered by record foreign outflows and elevated oil costs.

The Sensex shed 719 points on Monday, closing at 73,524. The Nifty fell 1% to 23,123, with 15 of 16 sectors declining. The MSCI Asia ex-Japan index tumbled 3.5%, South Korea's Kospi crashed 8.3%, and Japan's Nikkei lost 3.9%.

Analysts at Saxo Bank warned that "physical shortages may be measured in weeks rather than months" if the Hormuz blockade continues.

## What's Next

The immediate question is whether this pause becomes a lasting ceasefire or a brief intermission. The Trump administration is pursuing a memorandum of understanding with Iran that would reopen the strait, but talks remain stalled over Tehran's nuclear programme and demands for access to frozen funds. Iran insists any deal must include an end to Israel's operations in Lebanon.

For India, the calculus is straightforward: every week the strait stays closed costs the economy roughly ₹5,000 crore in additional fuel imports. Diplomatic language aside, New Delhi needs this war to end.

*Sources: Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Barron's, CNN-News18, Morningstar*
